Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Kofi Tonto says Ghana’s rent crisis has been neglected by successive governments, media Source : Emmanuel Tetteh 21 November 2026 9:16am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
A National Communications Member of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Kofi Tonto, says Ghana has neglected discussions on the country's rental challenges, blaming successive governments, the media, civil society and other national leadership for failing to give the issue the attention it deserves.
He has welcomed the renewed public debate on rent and accommodation, describing it as a positive development that should extend beyond the controversy over hostel charges at the University of Ghana.
Speaking on JoyNews' Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mr Tonto said although he was not entirely convinced by all the arguments advanced by the Rent Commissioner, he considered the official's interventions and the resulting public conversation a good starting point for addressing the country's rental challenges.
His comments come amid growing concerns over accommodation charges at the University of Ghana following a proposed 26 per cent increase by the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL).
The proposed adjustment was subsequently reduced after consultations with student leaders, but the development has triggered wider conversations about the affordability and availability of accommodation for students.
Mr Tonto observed that although the controversy over university hostels had helped bring rental issues into the national conversation, the challenges confronting tenants across the country were much broader.
He argued that rent had remained a major national concern but had not received adequate attention as a subject for sustained public discussion.
According to him, the country's rental challenges deserved to be examined beyond the immediate concerns of university students, given the wider implications for people seeking accommodation.
“I don't know if he is entirely right on all the issues, but I like him. I think it's a good start. Conversations on rent are long overdue,” he said.
Mr Tonto said the renewed attention to the subject should serve as an opportunity to address longstanding concerns within Ghana's rental sector.
He criticised what he described as the collective failure of national leadership to prioritise discussions on rent, identifying government, the media and civil society organisations as among those that had neglected the issue.
He said the lack of sustained engagement had been unfair to a subject that significantly affects the lives of Ghanaians.
“Maybe what has really necessitated this discussion on a big platform is the student hostels, it goes beyond that. The rent issues are so big and that, for me, is something we have been highly unfair to as a subject for discussion,” he added.
He further maintained that all major institutions and groups with the influence to shape national conversations had failed to address the matter adequately.
“Be it the government, be it the media, be it civil society, all forms of leadership in our country, we have all reneged on the discussion,” he said.
